title: Measure A: Origin, Governance, and Pavement Condition Trends
text: Measure A is El Cerrito’s half-cent transactions and use tax dedicated to street repair and maintenance, approved by voters on February 5, 2008. This page documents the tax’s original legal purpose, how its use has evolved, and the City’s pavement condition data from 2008 to the present.

title: Measure A: Origin, Governance, and Pavement Condition Trends
text:
Ballot Origin
Voters approved Measure A on February 5, 2008, formally titled “The El Cerrito Pothole Repair, Local Street Improvement and Maintenance Measure.” The tax was codified as Ordinance 2008-3, Municipal Code Chapter 4.60.

Ballot title and result sourced via secondary research citing Resolution 2008-14 (City certification of election results); not yet independently verified against the resolution itself.

title: Measure A: Origin, Governance, and Pavement Condition Trends
section: The Original Expenditure Plan (Exhibit 1 to Ordinance 2008-3)
text:
The Original Expenditure Plan (Exhibit 1 to Ordinance 2008-3)
The ordinance requires all tax proceeds be spent according to an Expenditure Plan attached as Exhibit 1. That Plan, still in force as codified, states:

“The Expenditure Plan is a simple one, as it proposes to utilize the one-half cent transactions and use tax for street maintenance and improvement-related purposes, rather than specific capital improvement projects.”

The Plan’s Accelerated Work Plan for the first five years is organized around exactly two categories, both pavement-focused:

Preparatory Work — crack sealing, structural pavement repairs, leveling/rideability corrections, ADA curb ramp installation, curb/gutter/sidewalk repair, temporary striping
Finish Resurfacing — final pavement surface and markings: overlay, micropaving, slurry seal, cape seal, striping and signage

The Plan set an explicit five-year target: bring the citywide PCI “up to or near 70.”
One category beyond pure pavement was built into the original Plan from the start: approximately 15% of tax revenue was set aside for “non-vehicular mobility and accessibility (curb ramps, improved striping) and significant drainage problems.” This was not a later addition — it appears in the original 2008 Exhibit 1.
Legal scope of the tax is broader than the Accelerated Work Plan’s named categories, however. Municipal Code §4.60.150(A) defines eligible spending to include an open-ended catch-all: “other such improvements as are deemed necessary by the city council for the benefit of the residents of the city.”
Debt limit: annual debt service may not exceed 75% of that year’s projected tax proceeds.

Source: Municipal Code Chapter 4.60, §4.60.150 and Exhibit 1 (Pavement Expenditure Plan), as codified from Ordinance 2008-3.

title: Measure A: Origin, Governance, and Pavement Condition Trends
text:
Governance Structure
The tax created a five-member Street Repair and Maintenance Citizens’ Oversight Committee, appointed by Council. Per Municipal Code §2.04.320, the committee’s role is explicitly and narrowly defined:

“The committee is not charged with decision-making on spending priorities, schedules, project details, funding source decisions… The committee shall serve in an advisory-only role to the city council.”

The committee reviews whether actual expenditures match the Council-approved Expenditure Plan; it does not set priorities or select projects. City staff and the City Attorney reiterated this narrow role repeatedly between 2008 and 2016 when committee members raised concerns about spending priorities.

Source: El Cerrito Municipal Code §2.04.320.

title: Measure A: Origin, Governance, and Pavement Condition Trends
section: The Funding Gap: What’s Needed vs. What’s Available
text:
The Funding Gap: What’s Needed vs. What’s Available
A separate 2023 scope-of-work document — for a City-commissioned 5-Year Paving Work Plan — puts the City’s own maintenance funding shortfall in stark terms:

“Combined with Gas Tax, Measure A, Measure J, and RMRA fund (SB1) for the City’s Street Improvement Fund (211), approximately $700,000 per year is available for street maintenance and rehabilitation. In the City’s PTAP 23 Pavement Management Program Report, approximately $1.9 million per year is required to maintain network PCI at current level 69. The City’s existing paving funding is insufficient to properly maintain its street network.”

In other words: pooling every available street-funding source — not Measure A alone — the City has access to roughly 37% of what its own consultant says is needed just to hold pavement condition steady at its current level. Not to improve it. To stop it from getting worse.
This is a different, broader funding pool than the Fund 211/Measure A-specific figures above (which combine Gas Tax, Measure A, Measure J, and SB1/RMRA together, rather than isolating Measure A’s own revenue), so the two shouldn’t be added together or treated as the same number — but together they show the same basic picture from two different angles: a dedicated street tax whose usable remainder, after debt service, is a shrinking share of what’s actually required.

title: Measure A: Origin, Governance, and Pavement Condition Trends
text:
Summary
Measure A’s original 2008 Expenditure Plan was pavement-focused, with a defined 15% carve-out for accessibility and drainage work built in from the outset. The ordinance’s legal text has not been amended since 2008. Beginning with a $100,000 diversion in August 2012 — a decision City staff explicitly acknowledged departed from the program’s stated original priorities, while remaining within the ordinance’s broad catch-all authorization — an increasing share of Measure A spending has gone to categories (traffic safety, neighborhood traffic management, Safe Routes to School, Complete Streets) not named in the original work plan. This shift was contested by some Citizens’ Oversight Committee members through 2014, then became an established, uncontested part of the program from 2016 onward. Separately, roughly $700,000 of the fund’s ~$2.3 million in annual revenue goes to bond debt service through 2036, leaving a variable remainder for actual street work. The City’s own 2023 consultant scope of work states that all combined street-funding sources together provide roughly $700,000 per year for maintenance and rehabilitation, against a stated requirement of $1.9 million per year just to hold pavement condition steady. Meanwhile, the City’s pavement condition, which reached the mid-80s during the initial accelerated program, has declined to 65 as of the most recent available data (mid-2025) — below the original plan’s five-year target of 70.

title: City Manager Compensation & Contract History
text:
Leave Benefits

Sick and vacation leave accrue at the same rate as other management employees, per Council resolution.
Executive/administrative leave: 75 hours credited each July 1 (37.5 hours in the first partial year). Upon termination or resignation, 100% of accumulated, unused administrative leave is paid out.
Standard paid holidays, floating holidays, birthday holiday, and bereavement leave, matching other management employees.
Upon termination (voluntary or involuntary), all accrued vacation, sick, and holiday leave is compensated at the then-current monthly salary rate — or, alternatively, applied toward CalPERS service credit if permitted.


Source: Third Amended Employment Agreement, Section 5.

title: City Manager Compensation & Contract History
text:
Termination & Severance

At-will employment: the City Manager serves at the pleasure of the Council and may be terminated at any time, with or without cause, subject to Charter restrictions. The agreement explicitly states this confers no property interest in continued employment.
Election-period protection: employment cannot be terminated during the 90 days before or after a City Council election, or during the 90 days following a change in Council membership (by election or appointment).
Severance: a lump-sum payment equal to 12 months’ base salary if the City terminates without cause or gives notice of non-renewal.
Resignation-at-Council-request clause: if the Council, by majority vote, asks the City Manager to resign, she is entitled to resign and still receive the same severance benefits as an involuntary termination without cause. This provision was first introduced in the 2020 amendment and has been carried forward in each subsequent version.
Abuse-of-office clawback: per Government Code §53243.2, any severance payment must be fully reimbursed to the City if the City Manager is later convicted of a crime involving abuse of office, as defined in §53243.4.


Source: Third Amended Employment Agreement, Sections 9, 10, and 11.

Professional development: the City budgets for travel, subsistence, and conference costs (League of California Cities, ICMA, California City Management Foundation, and similar organizations), plus membership dues for local civic/professional organizations.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
This is a standardized, source-based summary of the 37 unique meeting records supplied for the City of El Cerrito Citizen/Citizens Street Oversight Committee from September 2008 through December 2025. It is structured as source material for website development, with dates, meeting type, major financial and program information, actions, follow-up, and significance recorded in a consistent format.
Date convention: The meeting date is normalized from the meeting cover page and source filename. Several PDFs contain copied footer dates, OCR errors, or internal date inconsistencies; those have not been treated as separate meetings.
Source-file convention: Duplicate uploads are summarized only once. The two 2015 files uploaded again in the later batch are byte-for-byte duplicates of the earlier 2015 PDFs. The two December 15, 2025 PDFs have different file bytes but identical extracted meeting text, so they are treated as one meeting record.
Scope convention: The report summarizes the meeting minutes and identifies significant supporting packet material where it is included in the same PDF. DocuSign certificate pages are not treated as separate substantive records.
Record-gap convention: No 2017 meeting PDF was supplied. The September 24, 2018 minutes approve the September 26, 2016 minutes, but this report does not assume that no other 2017 meeting occurred. Likewise, only the supplied records are summarized for 2024 and 2025; a meeting that was scheduled in prior minutes is not treated as having occurred unless a corresponding source document was supplied.
Source-quality note: Where the official minutes contain an apparent copied or typographical inconsistency, this report preserves the supported substance and flags the inconsistency when it could matter to later publication. Examples include the May 10, 2021 action text referring to a “Fiscal Year 2020-21 Annual Report” under an agenda item labeled FY 2019-20, the June 23, 2022 certification line referring to 2023, and the November 13, 2023 PDF containing inconsistent footer/certification dates. The meeting dates used here follow the cover page and filename.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
September 22, 2008
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2008-09-22.pdf

Summary
This was the first meeting reflected in the supplied records. The committee organized itself, reviewed the ordinance establishing its role, and began defining how it would oversee Measure A street-improvement revenues and expenditures.


Key decisions and actions

Al Miller was elected chair unanimously.
Lynne Kessler was elected vice chair unanimously.
The committee reviewed the enabling ordinance, El Cerrito Municipal Code section 2.04.320, and discussed the committee’s role.
Staff agreed to obtain clarification on two apparent discrepancies between the ordinance and the Measure A Expenditure Plan.
The next meeting was scheduled for November 13, 2008, with a planned briefing on the background of the Measure A program.



Significance
The meeting established the committee’s basic governance and immediately identified an issue that would recur in later years: when language in the ordinance and the Expenditure Plan appears inconsistent, which document controls and how broad is the committee’s oversight role?

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
January 26, 2009
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2009-01-26.pdf

Summary
The committee received a detailed history of Measure A, reviewed the prior year’s audit materials, and clarified important questions about the committee’s authority and the types of expenses that could be charged to Measure A.


Key decisions and actions

The September 2008 minutes were approved, but members asked that future minutes summarize substantive discussion rather than record only actions.
Staff presented the history of the street program from the 2006 Street Condition Report through the February 2008 Measure A election.
On conflicts between the ordinance and the Expenditure Plan, staff advised that the ordinance controls.
The committee concurred that Measure A should not be charged for department administrators’ salaries.
The committee also accepted the interpretation that it does not establish spending priorities; its role is to review expenditures.
The committee reviewed FY 2007-08 audit and bond-related financial material.
The committee approved its annual report to the City Council.



Significance
This meeting established two core principles that appear repeatedly in later minutes: the ordinance governs when it conflicts with explanatory material, and the committee is primarily an expenditure-review body rather than a body that selects projects.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
July 27, 2009
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2009-07-27.pdf

Summary
The committee focused on how it should conduct its business, how Measure A sales-tax revenue is received and audited, and the scale and timing of the three-year street-resurfacing program.


Financial and program details

Finance staff explained that the local Measure A sales tax is accounted for separately from the regular Bradley-Burns sales tax.
After roughly ten months of FY 2008-09, Measure A revenue was reported at about $1.18 million against a projected $1.29 million for the year; staff expected the final result to be close to the projection.
The auditor explained transaction sampling and third-party confirmation of State sales-tax records.
Staff described a shift from a “comfort letter” to an Agreed Upon Procedures Report (AUPR) for bond-compliance reporting.
The 2009 program included rubberized asphalt overlay, asphalt-rubber cape seal, a federally funded overlay project, and storm-drain replacement at roughly 40–50 locations.
Staff projected that by the end of the accelerated bond program in 2010, approximately 87 percent of the city’s street surface would have been resurfaced.
Program expenditures over the three-year bond program were described as approaching $15 million, including some non-Measure-A funding and pre-Measure-A work.



Key decisions and actions

A proposed discussion of standing rules could not be acted on because it had not been placed on the published agenda; members discussed Brown Act requirements.
Members requested more detailed minutes, including motions, seconds and voting information. Staff said meetings would be audio recorded to assist in preparing minutes.
Staff agreed to provide a detailed fiscal-year expenditure list for committee review.
A September 28 meeting was scheduled for procedural issues, with the annual audit review planned for January.



Significance
The meeting shows the committee moving from organizational questions toward detailed fiscal oversight while the large, bond-funded resurfacing program was still underway.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
September 28, 2009
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2009-09-28.pdf

Summary
The committee developed more formal operating procedures and clarified what underlying financial records it wanted to review in carrying out its oversight responsibilities.


Key topics

Members worked from draft standing rules and relevant Municipal Code provisions.
The committee concluded that its oversight should include State revenue statements, revenue and expenditure reports, and samples of invoices and other transaction-level documents.
Members also discussed the ability to request underlying documents used by the City’s auditors.
The committee concluded that reviewing actual revenue information was necessary even though the ordinance principally directs it to review expenditures of revenues.
The committee discussed whether minutes or other documents should be signed and whether meeting audio recordings are public records that must be retained.



Follow-up

Staff was to determine whether signatures should be placed on committee documents.
Staff was to determine the public-record/retention status of meeting audio recordings.
Sample invoices and additional State revenue documentation were to be brought to a future meeting.
The next meeting was scheduled for November 9, 2009.



Significance
This meeting formalized the committee’s preference for source-document review rather than relying only on high-level financial summaries.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
November 9, 2009
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2009-11-09.pdf

Summary
The committee followed up on records-management questions, reviewed the financing structure of the Street Improvement Fund, and examined sample contractor and consultant invoices.


Financial and program details

Staff described annual Measure A revenue as approximately $1.3 million.
About $750,000 per year was expected to go to bond debt service, leaving approximately $550,000 for street projects and other necessary expenses once the large bond proceeds were exhausted.
The first three years included approximately $10.5 million in bond proceeds.
The bonds were structured for repayment over 30 years.
The City’s finance system showed approximately $1.348 million in FY 2008-09 Measure A sales-tax revenue versus a budget of about $1.29 million.
A State Controller report appeared lower because of fiscal-year cash timing, but staff explained that after accrual of the final FY 2008-09 revenues, the State and City figures reconciled.



Key decisions and actions

Staff reported that there was no general City standard requiring signatures on minutes or resolutions. The annual report to the City Council, however, had been signed by the chair.
Approved minutes were to have the draft watermark removed, be transmitted for website posting, and be kept in the committee’s official file.
Staff stated that meeting proceedings, minutes and materials are public records.
The draft standing rules were reviewed but action was deferred until all members could participate.
The committee reviewed sample construction and project-management invoices to understand how payments connect to Measure A accounts.



Significance
The meeting provides a useful explanation of the long-term Measure A financing model: a large initial bond-funded rehabilitation program followed by a much smaller annual pay-as-you-go maintenance capacity while debt service continues.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
January 25, 2010
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2010-01-25.pdf

Summary
The committee adopted formal standing rules, reviewed the FY 2008-09 audit and AUPR, and discussed how Measure A restrictions interact with bond covenants and other funding sources in the Street Improvement Fund.


Key decisions and actions

Al Miller was re-elected chair and Lynne Kessler vice chair.
The committee unanimously adopted its standing rules. Those rules established a regular meeting schedule while preserving the ability to call special meetings.
The FY 2008-09 State Controller revenue figure was reconciled to the City’s general ledger at $1,348,938.
The committee discussed a bond-covenant provision that could allow excess bond funds to be transferred after projects were complete. Staff and the committee distinguished that provision from the City’s Measure A ordinance, which continued to restrict use of Measure A funds.
The committee discussed how Measure A and non-Measure-A revenues are commingled in the Street Improvement Fund and why the committee could still evaluate whether Measure A money was used for eligible street work.
The committee approved its annual report to the City Council.



Significance
The committee’s standing rules were now formally in place, and the meeting clarified that bond documents do not expand the purposes for which the City’s tax ordinance permits Measure A revenues to be spent.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
September 27, 2010
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2010-09-27.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed the near-completion of the initial Measure A resurfacing program, the FY 2009-10 financial activity, and the long-term consequences of the bond repayment structure.


Pavement-program details

Staff reported that approximately 80 percent of City streets would have been resurfaced by completion of the current program.
The program included 43 storm-drain locations, described as roughly 3 percent of Measure A program costs.
Nearly 400 curb ramps were described as about 9 percent of program costs, below the originally projected 15 percent share for accessibility and related improvements.



Financial details

FY 2009-10 Measure A sales-tax receipts were approximately $1.3 million.
No new bond revenue was received that year; the bond proceeds had been received in 2008.
The committee noted that the expenditure listing did not include the roughly $738,000 annual debt-service payment.
Staff explained that about 60 percent of annual Measure A proceeds would be committed to debt repayment over the 30-year bond term, leaving roughly 40 percent for ongoing maintenance until the bonds are retired.



Key decisions and actions

The committee reviewed a detailed FY 2009-10 expenditure list before the audit.
Members asked for a clearer “paper trail” showing the relationship among the ordinance, City Council authorization, project execution, expenditures, and committee review. Staff agreed to consider creating a flow chart.
The November 2010 meeting was cancelled unanimously.
The next regular meeting was set for January 24, 2011.



Significance
This meeting marks the transition from the intensive initial repaving program toward the long-term maintenance era, in which debt service absorbs most annual Measure A revenue.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
January 24, 2011
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2011-01-24.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed the FY 2009-10 audit, received a pavement-program update, elected officers, and approved its annual report.


Key topics and actions

Staff clarified that curbs and gutters, sidewalks, and traffic-control items can fall within the Measure A program even though pavement rehabilitation was the primary objective presented to voters.
Al Miller was elected chair and Liz Ozselcuk vice chair.
The auditor reviewed the FY 2009-10 AUPR and reported no compliance findings or other issues requiring committee attention.
The committee discussed the auditor’s sampling procedures, revenue categories, bond covenants and the presence of non-Measure-A money in the Street Improvement Fund.
The annual report to the City Council was approved unanimously.



Significance
The audit review found no compliance problems, while the discussion continued to distinguish the program’s primary pavement purpose from other street-system uses permitted under Measure A.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
October 10, 2011
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2011-10-10.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed FY 2010-11 revenues and expenditures, discussed the City’s improved pavement condition, and opened a significant discussion over its standing rules after a previously scheduled meeting had been cancelled.


Pavement and financial details

Staff reported a most-recent Pavement Condition Index (PCI) of 85, while noting that the regional “Pothole Report” used a three-year average that still reflected earlier, lower conditions.
Preliminary FY 2010-11 Street Improvement Fund revenues were approximately $2.1 million.
An $83,000 EBMUD payment represented its share of Balra Drive repairs after water-line work.
Expenditures included salaries for two temporary project staff who had taken over work previously performed by the outside project-management firm.



Key topics and actions

Members discussed what portions of the street system should be considered within Measure A, including curbs, gutters, sidewalks, traffic-control items and signage.
The committee discussed concern about the cancellation of a regular meeting and whether the standing rules gave too much practical control to the staff liaison.
The committee directed the liaison to provide legally required notice for the next regular meeting and place revision of the standing rules on the agenda.



Significance
The meeting combined financial oversight with a governance dispute about the committee’s independence and its ability to meet when staff is unavailable.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
November 14, 2011
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2011-11-14.pdf

Summary
The committee clarified which City staff costs may legitimately be charged to Measure A and undertook a detailed review of proposed revisions to its standing rules.


Measure A cost-allocation details

Staff reported that costs related to decommissioning the temporary City Hall campus had been moved out of the Streets Fund (Fund 211) and into the Capital Fund (Fund 301).
Staff reaffirmed that general administrative salaries should not be charged to Measure A.
Direct project work—such as planning, design, construction administration and project management—could be eligible even when performed by City staff rather than consultants.
Staff time was to be documented through time cards.
The chair asked staff to develop a written policy or procedure and obtain City Attorney guidance on eligible staff costs.



Standing-rules discussion
The committee reviewed proposed rules concerning: - cancellation and rescheduling of meetings; - appointment of an acting secretary if no staff liaison is present; - whether the committee may conduct business without staff; - escalation to the City Manager and then City Council if a liaison fails to perform required duties; - Brown Act compliance; - severability of rules; - officer nominations and elections; - limits on consecutive terms for officers; and - periodic review of the standing rules.


Follow-up
Staff was to prepare a revised draft and consult the City Attorney on unresolved legal questions before the January meeting.


Significance
The meeting is important both for defining eligible personnel costs and for formalizing protections for the committee’s ability to function independently of any single staff liaison.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
January 23, 2012
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2012-01-23.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed the FY 2010-11 audit, refined its policy understanding regarding staff costs, elected officers, and completed another round of standing-rules revisions.


Financial details

The AUPR reported no findings or exceptions requiring corrective action.
State Controller Measure A revenue was reported as $1,375,828.
FY 2010-11 expenditures shown in the financial statements were $2,579,920.
Staff estimated cumulative Measure A expenditures since inception at roughly $14–15 million.
A year-end “Due to Other Funds” balance was explained as temporary borrowing caused by additional authorized work on the 2010 contract, including Balra Drive.



Staff-cost policy

Direct project-related staff work could be charged to Measure A when it substitutes for work that otherwise would have been performed by consultants or contractors.
Routine administrative work by Public Works support staff or indirect work by Finance, Legal or Personnel was not to be charged.
The Public Works Director’s time might occasionally qualify if directly tied to project work, but staff expected that to be unusual.



Key decisions and actions

The annual report was approved unanimously.
Al Miller was elected chair; Lynne Kessler was elected vice chair.
The committee amended its standing rules after receiving City Attorney input, including language addressing meetings without staff, severability, officer nominations, and continuation of incumbent officers when replacements cannot be selected.
The next regular meeting was set for September 24, 2012.



Significance
This meeting provides one of the clearest statements in the record separating eligible direct project labor from ineligible administrative overhead.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
September 24, 2012
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2012-09-24.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed FY 2011-12 revenues and expenditures, discussed the City’s excavation-moratorium program, and considered the next phase of pavement maintenance after the large initial rehabilitation program.


Financial details

Total revenue was reported as $1,519,355.
Annual bond debt service was $737,582, leaving roughly $750,000 for annual work.
The 2010 pavement-condition report had estimated annual pavement needs at approximately $500,000.
Overall revenues exceeded expenditures by about $350,000, leaving a modest surplus for the next fiscal year.
The City’s matching contribution for an MTC pavement-management grant was approximately $4,086 on a grant exceeding $20,000.
A GIS addition to the pavement-management system cost $2,720.
A contractor claim of roughly $88,000 from an older paving project was settled for $45,000.
The School District reimbursed the City $19,296.90 for traffic-calming improvements near Fairmont School.



Program details

Major street work was described as nearly complete.
Eureka near Fairmont School and Carquinez were identified as streets not paved during the major program and possible future candidates.
Staff cited potential future paving grants of approximately $460,000 and $350,000, with local matching requirements.
The excavation moratorium was described as five years after an overlay and three years after slurry/cape seal work.
The fee for the City to perform required slurry-seal restoration after an allowed excavation was $570.
The summer/fall FY 2012-13 paving program was deferred until spring 2013, primarily because of limited staff resources.



Key decisions and actions

The standing rules were approved as version 2012-2.
The November meeting was cancelled because no business was planned.
The next meeting was set for January 28, 2013.



Significance
The minutes show the City beginning to shift from large-scale rehabilitation to recurring maintenance while still carrying substantial annual debt service.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
January 28, 2013
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2013-01-28.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed the FY 2011-12 audit, discussed the emerging dispute over use of Measure A for traffic projects, received a new pavement-condition forecast, and elected new officers.


Financial and audit details

Audited revenue differed from the preliminary September presentation because a final State payment of approximately $63,000 was received after the earlier statements; some reimbursements were also reclassified from negative expenditures to revenues.
The annual report was approved unanimously.



Pavement details

The draft 2012 pavement report showed an average PCI of 85, unchanged from the 2010 report.
The biennial pavement-condition study cost approximately $25,000; MTC grant funding covered all but about $4,000, with the Measure A program paying the local portion.
The draft report estimated approximately $4.37 million would be needed over five years to achieve the best feasible street conditions, compared with $2.6 million in the 2010 report. Staff attributed the increase largely to higher pavement-construction costs.



Governance and policy issues

Lynne Kessler asked about City Council’s reallocation of Measure A money to neighborhood traffic projects.
Staff said those traffic projects were eligible under Measure A; Thomas Miller objected that the use was inconsistent with what voters primarily expected the tax to fund.
Jerry Bradshaw announced his retirement from full-time City employment and said Yvetteh Ortiz would assume the committee-liaison role.
Aurelia Schultz was elected chair and Lynne Kessler vice chair.



Significance
This meeting marks the beginning of a sustained 2013–2014 dispute over the boundary between pavement spending and other street-safety uses of Measure A.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
September 23, 2013
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2013-09-23.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed FY 2012-13 activity, examined the FY 2013-14 work plan, received a Brown Act refresher, and was shown how Measure A project authorization flows from the ordinance and budget process through final audit and committee review.


Major topics

Chair Aurelia Schultz had resigned; Vice Chair Lynne Kessler and the remaining members attended.
Thomas Miller reiterated concern that Measure A was being used for purposes other than pavement, curbs and gutters. Because the issue had not been agendized, substantive action was deferred under the Brown Act.
Staff reviewed FY 2012-13 revenues and expenditures and noted that certain Board of Equalization corrections were still pending.



FY 2013-14 work-plan details
Staff described five Measure A-related capital projects, including: - $50,000 in matching funds for the Arlington Curve at Brewster Drive safety project; - the Traffic Safety & Management Program; - a State paving project with approximately $354,000 in Prop. 1B funding and approximately $478,000 in Measure A local matching funds; - a federally funded paving project requiring Caltrans approvals; and - an annual paving project that had not yet been fully scoped.


Project-approval process
Staff presented a process beginning with Municipal Code section 4.60.150 and the Measure A Expenditure Plan, continuing through the annual Capital Improvement Program budget and project/contract approval, and ending with fiscal close, independent audit and committee review.


Supporting material in the PDF
The file includes substantial packet material following the meeting minutes, including Brown Act presentation material and documents illustrating the project-approval and Measure A allocation process.


Significance
This record is particularly useful for explaining the mechanics of how a Measure A project moves from legal authorization to budget appropriation, construction, financial close and oversight review.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
November 4, 2013
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2013-11-04.pdf

Summary
This meeting was devoted primarily to whether Measure A money could properly be used for non-pavement projects and whether those uses were consistent with voter intent.


Key factual background

Staff reviewed the Measure A ordinance and Expenditure Plan.
A staff report to the City Council dated August 21, 2012 had recommended $100,000 of Measure A funding for a Traffic Safety & Management Program.
Staff identified that as the first time Measure A money had been approved for non-pavement work.
Staff stated that pavement improvements remained the first priority, but that substantial progress on pavement allowed a modest share of funds to support other purposes authorized by Measure A.



Committee debate

Lynne Kessler and Thomas Miller argued that traffic-project spending conflicted with the spirit of what voters were told, even if broad ordinance language could be read to permit it.
Al Miller emphasized the ordinance and City Council’s authority to adopt an annual expenditure plan within the authorized purposes.
The committee discussed Expenditure Plan language referring to approximately 15 percent of tax revenue for non-vehicular mobility/accessibility and significant drainage problems; staff said curb-ramp work during the major program had amounted to about 9 percent.
The committee also revisited administrative-cost language that conflicted with the ordinance’s restriction on administrative salaries.



Follow-up
The regular November 11 meeting had already been cancelled because of Veterans Day. The next regular meeting was expected on January 27, 2014.


Significance
This is a central document for understanding the later controversy over Measure A: it contains both the City’s legal/programmatic rationale and the objections of committee members who believed the spending departed from the voters’ primary understanding.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
January 27, 2014
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2014-01-27.pdf

Summary
The committee held a lengthy discussion about non-pavement Measure A spending, voter intent, transparency, whether the measure should be amended, and the narrow post-expenditure role assigned to the committee.


Measure A funding discussion

Thomas Miller argued that the City’s use of Measure A for certain non-pavement projects was inconsistent with what voters expected and argued that the matter should be returned to voters.
Lynne Kessler’s principal concern was that the committee had not been informed promptly when staff recommended reallocating funds.
Al Miller argued that the measure and ordinance expressly included categories beyond pavement, such as accessibility, bicycle, crosswalk, striping and signage improvements.
City Attorney Sky Woodruff described the committee as a post-expenditure review body: City Council adopts the eligible expenditure plan and budget; the committee later reviews whether actual spending conforms to what Council authorized under Measure A.



Financial context

Staff stated that approximately $14.8 million of Measure A funds had been spent since inception and had helped leverage approximately $2.8 million in grant funding.
In a group of four highlighted projects, approximately $618,000 of Measure A funding was associated with projects totaling about $15.5 million; staff described the Measure A share as helping leverage substantial outside grant funding.



Other topics

The annual audit and annual report were delayed because the citywide audit was not yet complete.
Staff explained the Traffic Safety & Management Program, including speed-feedback and traffic-calming measures used on streets such as Arlington and Barrett.
Staff reported that El Cerrito had received regional recognition for improved street conditions; the PCI was approximately 84, compared with a condition in the high 40s during the period before Measure A.



Significance
This meeting contains the most extensive discussion in the supplied set about the committee’s legal authority, voter intent and whether it should be involved before or only after City Council spending decisions.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
April 3, 2014
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2014-04-03.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed the FY 2012-13 audit, approved a divided annual report, and continued the debate over the permissible uses of Measure A and the committee’s authority.


Audit findings

The auditor explained the Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) and the AUPR.
All original bond proceeds had been spent, so future AUPR work would focus more directly on whether expenditures complied with continuing restrictions.
The auditor reported that tested expenditures were consistent with City Council directives and Measure A limitations and identified no exceptions requiring corrective action.
Finance staff said the CAFR notes should be included in future agenda packets because they contain important detail on transfers and fund activity.



Annual report

The committee approved the annual report to City Council by a 3-2 vote.
Al Miller, Elizabeth Ozselcuk and Matthew Kelly voted yes; Chair Thomas Miller and Vice Chair Lynne Kessler voted no.
The approved report was to reflect that it had been adopted by a divided vote.



Committee-role discussion

Public speakers and committee members discussed Brown Act procedure, agenda wording and the scope of the committee’s authority.
The City Attorney reiterated that the committee’s task is to evaluate whether expenditures match the City Council’s approved Measure A expenditure plan, not to decide which otherwise-lawful projects Council should fund.



Significance
This meeting is notable because the disagreement over Measure A policy was reflected in a formal 3-2 split on the annual report, even though the independent audit itself reported no exceptions.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee

April 27, 2015

Summary
The committee reviewed the FY 2013-14 audit, developed a clearer way to track City Council-authorized Measure A expenditures, received a pavement-program update, and elected new officers.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
September 28, 2015
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2015-09-28.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed preliminary FY 2014-15 financial activity and the updated Expenditure Plan Status Report, examined the FY 2015-16 budget and project plan, and discussed the Traffic Safety & Management Program and an upcoming slurry-seal/curb-ramp project.


FY 2014-15 review

Staff presented the revised Expenditure Plan Status Report and preliminary financial activity.
Committee members clarified that project totals may include grants and other funds, but the committee’s oversight responsibility is specifically for Measure A revenue.
Members questioned the accounting label “Miscellaneous Professional Services.” Staff explained that the category included specialized work such as engineering, design, project management, construction management, geotechnical services and materials testing. Staff distributed City Council agenda bills and supporting material for the adopted budget and Measure A expenditure plan.
The Traffic Safety & Management Program included work under the Neighborhood Traffic Management Program and speed-feedback signs on streets including Arlington Boulevard, Central Avenue and Barrett Avenue.

Committee members asked that future descriptions of Measure A projects be clearer and suggested that future budget resolutions expressly state that the listed expenditures are consistent with Measure A.

Slurry-seal and curb-ramp project

Staff reported that construction bids for the 2015 Slurry Seal and Curb Ramp Project were higher than estimated.

The meeting shows the committee’s oversight process becoming more documentation-focused: members wanted project descriptions, accounting categories and Council authorization language to make it easier for the public to understand exactly how Measure A money was budgeted and spent.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:
May 9, 2016
Meeting type: Special meeting
Source file: 2016-05-09.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed the FY 2014-15 audit and Agreed Upon Procedures Report, revisited the definition of the committee’s oversight role, reviewed the FY 2015-16 Expenditure Plan, and received an update on the 2016 resurfacing program.


Audit and financial details

Committee Member Al Miller objected to language in Audit Note 8.C that appeared to describe a broader committee role. Staff Liaison Yvetteh Ortiz confirmed that the committee’s purpose is to oversee the proper expenditure of Measure A funds and does not include setting priorities or making recommendations; she said the language would be corrected in future reports.
Compared with the preliminary figures reviewed in September 2015, audited FY 2014-15 tax revenue was lower by $100,200 because revenue had been booked to FY 2014-15 that properly belonged in FY 2015-16.
Grant revenue increased in the audited figures.
Additional administrative expenses appeared for preparation of the AUPR, legal notices and printing; those costs had previously been shown under individual projects.
The committee again discussed the general-ledger label “Miscellaneous Professional Services.” Because the Finance Director had recently departed, the issue was left for later review.



Annual report to City Council

Staff revised the committee’s annual report to clarify that the Expenditure Plan is approved by the City Council.
The draft also requested that future City Council budget resolutions include a “whereas” clause confirming the appropriate use of Measure A funds.
The committee asked for language acknowledging and supporting that, when Council adopts resolutions authorizing Measure A budget amendments, it is confirming that those expenditures are an appropriate use of the funds.
The committee unanimously approved the report with that revision and authorized final review by the chair for presentation at the June 7, 2016 City Council meeting.



FY 2015-16 program details

Staff provided the requested project-information sheet for the Traffic Safety & Management Program, Project C3070.
Staff reviewed a mid-year adjustment for Project C3074, the 2014 Pavement Rehabilitation/Manila Trees item; encumbered carryover; reconciliation between accounting-system figures and the approved Expenditure Plan; and additional federal grant revenue.
The 2016 resurfacing project was in design, with final street segments still being selected. Final design was anticipated in June and construction in summer 2016.
New curb-ramp requirements associated with resurfacing were increasing project costs.
Staff was considering microsurfacing instead of slurry seal because of its faster drying time.



Governance

The committee discussed two vacant seats and the lack of applications.
Matthew Kelly and Marlene Keller were continued as chair and vice-chair through 2016.
The next meeting was scheduled for September 26, 2016.

The meeting reinforced the committee’s narrow post-expenditure oversight role while also improving the wording of the annual report so that City Council’s responsibility for deciding whether planned expenditures are permissible under Measure A was more explicit.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee
text:

Source file: 2016-09-26.pdf

Summary
The committee reviewed preliminary FY 2015-16 financial activity, received the FY 2016-17 Expenditure Plan and paving work plan, and discussed how grant money should be tracked when used together with Measure A funds.

FY 2016-17 program

Staff presented the City’s FY 2016-17 and FY 2017-18 Biennial Budget material relating to Measure A.
The 2016 Microsurfacing and Curb Ramp Project, approved by Council through an August 2016 budget amendment, represented the principal paving work plan for FY 2016-17.

Two committee vacancies remained.
The Standing Rules were reviewed; no action was taken.
Staff noted that November meetings had often served as placeholders and might be cancelled if no business required action.
The January 2017 audit meeting was expected to be delayed, probably until April or May, because of the timing of the City’s audit reports.

This meeting contains an important accounting-policy development: future grant revenue was to be placed in a separate fund rather than mixed with Measure A activity, making the committee’s tax-fund oversight easier to follow.

title: City of El Cerrito Citizens Street Oversight Committee

September 24, 2018
Meeting type: Regular meeting
Source file: 2018-09-24.pdf

Summary
After the gap in the supplied records, the committee reviewed two fiscal years of audited information, discussed the 2017 refinancing of the original Measure A debt, reviewed the FY 2017-18 Expenditure Plan, and elected officers.


FY 2015-16 audit

Finance Director Mark Rasiah reviewed the Street Improvement Fund, Measure A revenues and the original 2008 bonds.

Staff explained that the program had moved from the accelerated rehabilitation phase after the 2008 bond issue into a maintenance phase.
Audited FY 2015-16 tax revenues were higher than the preliminary figures because of a one-year revenue spike.
Audited expenses were lower than the preliminary figures because approximately $446,000 of costs associated with the 2013-14 Pavement Rehabilitation Project, C3074, were moved to FY 2014-15.
Committee members asked about the negative fund balance; staff, Finance and the auditor explained that fund deficits can occur even though the City does not normally budget for them.
The committee unanimously approved the FY 2015-16 report for later presentation to City Council.



FY 2016-17 audit

Staff presented the FY 2016-17 Expenditure Plan Status Report and audited financial activity.
Auditor Ahmed Badawi reported no exceptions in the AUPR.
The auditor highlighted a lower debt-service payment associated with the timing of the 2017 bond reissuance and cautioned that the payment would not remain that low in the next year.
Staff explained that Project C3027 had been used to track annual street-improvement projects since 2007.
Pavement-condition assessments were described as recurring every two to three years and as the starting point for annual project selection, subject to more detailed engineering and pavement testing.
The committee unanimously approved the FY 2016-17 report for presentation to City Council.



FY 2017-18 and governance

Staff presented the FY 2017-18 Expenditure Plan Status Report, including annual budget approvals and subsequent mid-year adjustments.
The Standing Rules were reviewed. Members discussed changing regular meeting dates and asked for City Attorney clarification about concurrent service on other City boards, commissions or committees.
Matthew Kelly was continued as chair; Vanessa Hill was elected vice-chair.
Because the regular November date fell on Veterans Day, the committee set November 14, 2018 as its next meeting date.

This meeting reconnects the financial record after the 2016–2018 gap and documents the transition from the original 2008 bonds to the 2017 refinancing while preserving the committee’s annual audit-review process.

Summary
The committee reviewed the FY 2017-18 audit, examined debt and refinancing questions, and received updates on the FY 2018-19 and FY 2019-20 expenditure plans.

September 28, 2020

Summary
The committee reviewed preliminary FY 2019-20 finances and adopted two important changes to its Standing Rules: moving the regular audit meeting from January to May and making review of source documents discretionary rather than mandatory.


FY 2019-20 financial review

Staff presented unaudited revenues and expenditures and compared budget to actual results.
Revenue sources included Measure A sales tax and restoration fees.
Expense categories included debt service, legal and financial expenses, City personnel expenses outside capital projects, and capital projects.
Staff provided the requested information on Public Works personnel allocated to Measure A.
Committee questions covered:

fiscal-year accrual of sales-tax revenue;
work performed by Public Works personnel outside capital projects;
the basis for personnel allocations;
COVID-19 administrative leave;
consultant expenses within the annual street program;
minority- and women-owned-business contracting requirements; and
improvements in the Korematsu Safe Routes to School project.

The chair requested future expenditure totals for each subproject within the annual street-improvement program.



FY 2020-21 plan

Staff presented the FY 2020-21 Expenditure Plan adopted by Council in June 2020.

This meeting materially modernized the committee’s operating rules to match actual audit timing and reduced the procedural burden of mandatory source-document review.

title: Cost & Funding History
section: The Gap Between Internal Knowledge and Public Disclosure
text:
The Gap Between Internal Knowledge and Public Disclosure
The Impact Report itself states that the $37,224,000 Scenario 3 figure was finalized only after the January 20, 2026 study session and was not the number presented live at that meeting (Impact Report, p.24) — meaning the most current, precise cost figure was not made public until the February 19, 2026 Impact Report, roughly one month after the January 20 session and many months after the petition (using the ~$21.2M figure) had already been circulated and signed (petition filed November 20, 2025).
Whether City staff possessed a $37M-range estimate before the November 2025 petition filing is the central question in the “known but undisclosed” argument. The documented record supports: the City engaged Griffin Structures as Owner’s Representative starting April 1, 2025 — before the May 6, 2025 Notice of Intent, and well before the November 20, 2025 petition filing — specifically to provide updated TOD cost information.

Strongest documented evidence available: as of January 20, 2026, staff already had a $35–48M range in hand (Agenda Bill 8.B), well above the ~$21.2M petition figure. This range is dated to the Jan. 20, 2026 staff report; an earlier-dated internal document proving the City had this range specifically before the Nov. 20, 2025 petition filing has not been confirmed. Any public claim should be limited to what’s provable from dated documents, pending further records request.

title: Cost & Funding History
text:
Other Financing Facts

Special election cost commonly cited at $80,000 for the consolidated June 2 date. Per the Jan. 20, 2026 agenda bill, a standalone (non-consolidated) special election would have cost $213,768–$267,210, versus $3–4.50/registered voter (roughly $53,000–$80,000) if consolidated with the June 2 statewide primary — the $80,000 figure is the high end of the consolidated-election estimate, not the standalone cost. (Agenda Bill 8.A, 1/20/2026, p.1)
Tax collection start: per the Impact Report’s legal analysis, earliest realistic start was the 2026-27 tax year, with an Effective Date potentially as early as July 31, 2026 (Impact Report, p.11–12), contingent on County certification in time for the Council’s July 21, 2026 regular meeting. Actual tax bills (ad valorem mechanics) go out in the fall and are due December 10 / April 10 (Impact Report, p.12).
Comparable benchmark: current library’s existing annual operating/maintenance cost is $157,615 (Impact Report, p.19).

NoteA Note on Sources



This page synthesizes City of El Cerrito budget and audit documents, official California state records, and appellate case research. A California Public Records Act request has been submitted to the City Clerk to obtain several underlying documents that are currently available only secondhand (see “What Remains Unverified” below). title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
text:
Executive Summary
California abolished redevelopment agencies (RDAs) statewide in 2011–2012 to redirect growing property tax revenue back to schools, counties, and cities’ general funds, and to reduce the state’s own budget obligations under Proposition 98. El Cerrito’s RDA was dissolved effective February 1, 2012, along with more than 400 others statewide.
Separately, El Cerrito’s RDA and City government, in the window between Governor Brown’s January 2011 proposal to eliminate RDAs and the law’s actual passage in June 2011, moved roughly $1.98 million in cash, $400,243 in bond proceeds, and about $10.17 million in real property from the RDA to the Municipal Services Corporation (MSC), a nonprofit the City itself controls. A City staff memorandum from the time described the purpose as helping to “protect tax increment revenue.”
The California Department of Finance determined this transfer was not legally effective, because the MSC was financially controlled by the City. It ordered $1,981,989 in cash returned. El Cerrito fought this in court for nearly eight years and lost, with the Third District Court of Appeal affirming the state’s position in March 2021.
El Cerrito was not alone in attempting this kind of maneuver — Tracy, Brentwood, Big Bear Lake, and San Bernardino all did something similar and were subject to the same clawback process.
Two distinct dollar figures come up in City financial records, and conflating them produces a misleading picture:

$1,981,989 — the total amount the state Department of Finance determined El Cerrito owed, fully repaid by 2018.
$1,321,189 — a separate, internal accounting balance: money the City’s General Fund advanced to the Successor Agency to help make those payments, written off in FY2020-21 once it became clear it would never be repaid internally. This was not an additional payment to the state — it was General Fund cash already spent, formally acknowledged as a loss.

A concrete, ongoing legacy of the dispute persists: as of a March 2024 City budget item, El Cerrito was still resolving a $350,000 obligation to the MSC — incurred in 2016 to help finance the state repayment — by directing General Fund money to a City infrastructure project.

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 1 — What Was a Redevelopment Agency, and Why Did Cities Want One?
text:
Part 1 — What Was a Redevelopment Agency, and Why Did Cities Want One?
Starting in the 1940s, California law allowed cities to form Redevelopment Agencies (RDAs) — separate government entities dedicated to fixing up “blighted” areas: rundown commercial corridors, underused industrial land, and similar areas the city wanted to revitalize. El Cerrito’s RDA project area covered 368 acres, mainly along San Pablo Avenue, and had been in place since 1977.

The core mechanism: tax increment financing
RDAs were funded through a tool called tax increment financing:

When an RDA project area was created, the property tax revenue coming from that area at that moment was “frozen” as a baseline.
As redevelopment occurred and property values rose, the growth in property tax revenue above that baseline — the “increment” — went to the RDA, instead of being split among the normal recipients: school districts, the county, special districts, and the city’s own general fund.
The RDA could spend that increment directly, or borrow against future increment by issuing bonds.

This meant an RDA project area effectively diverted a growing share of local property tax revenue into a dedicated pot controlled by the city, for redevelopment purposes — money that, absent the RDA, would have flowed through the normal formula and given every taxing entity, including the city’s own general fund, its usual proportional share of the growth.

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 2 — Why Did the State Eliminate RDAs in 2011–2012?
text:
Part 2 — Why Did the State Eliminate RDAs in 2011–2012?
By 2011, California had more than 400 RDAs statewide, collectively capturing a large and steadily growing share of property tax revenue. This mattered directly to the state budget because of Proposition 98, which guarantees a minimum funding level for schools: when RDAs diverted property tax away from school districts, the state had to backfill the lost school funding from the state general fund. RDAs were, in effect, quietly costing the state billions of dollars a year in backfill obligations during a severe state budget crisis.
Governor Jerry Brown proposed eliminating RDAs statewide in his January 10, 2011 budget. The Legislature passed the dissolution law, Assembly Bill 1X 26 (“ABX1 26”), on June 28, 2011. The California Supreme Court upheld the law in California Redevelopment Association v. Matosantos (December 2011). RDAs were formally dissolved statewide effective February 1, 2012.

The 2011 Governor’s Budget Summary framed RDA elimination as redirecting property tax growth toward core public services — schools, counties, and cities — rather than a permanently growing, dedicated redevelopment pot. (Source: Governor’s Budget Summary 2011-12, Jan. 10, 2011, redevelopment discussion at p. 28.)

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 3 — The Transition Period: Why This Story Is Complicated
text:
Part 3 — The Transition Period: Why This Story Is Complicated
The most confusing part of this history — and the part that matters most for understanding El Cerrito — is the roughly thirteen-month gap between when dissolution became a known threat (January 2011) and when it actually took legal effect (February 2012). During that window, RDAs were still fully legal entities that could sign agreements, spend money, and move assets.
Many cities and their RDAs used this window to try to lock in resources before dissolution took effect — signing agreements that committed RDA funds to specific projects, or transferring RDA-owned cash, bonds, and property to other entities. This was a well-documented statewide pattern, not something unique to El Cerrito.
The dissolution law anticipated this. It created a state review process — the Due Diligence Review (DDR), run by the Department of Finance, alongside a separate Asset Transfer Review by the State Controller’s Office — that examined every former RDA’s transactions going back to January 1, 2011. Its purpose was to identify and reverse any transfers made during the transition window that amounted to moving RDA resources beyond the reach of the dissolution law, particularly transfers to entities that were nominally independent but actually controlled by the sponsoring city.

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 5 — Why Did El Cerrito Owe $1.98 Million?
text:
Part 5 — Why Did El Cerrito Owe $1.98 Million?
This is the single most important question to understand, and the answer is not that the state imposed a new tax, fine, or penalty. It is that the state determined El Cerrito had moved money it was not legally allowed to move, and ordered it returned.

Before dissolution, El Cerrito’s RDA legitimately held cash from its tax-increment revenue.
In early 2011, anticipating dissolution, the RDA transferred that cash — along with bond proceeds and property — to the Municipal Services Corporation, a nonprofit the City itself created and controls.
The dissolution law specifically prohibited RDAs from simply handing their assets to their sponsoring city during this period; the whole point of the law was to prevent RDA resources from becoming a windfall for cities rather than flowing back to the normal, shared property-tax distribution.
The Department of Finance’s Due Diligence Review concluded that the MSC was not a genuinely independent third party — it was financially controlled by the City — so under the law’s own definitions, transferring RDA assets to the MSC was legally equivalent to transferring them to the City itself, which was not permitted.
DOF therefore ordered the $1,981,989 in cash returned, so it could go through the normal redistribution process (the RPTTF) that sends property tax to schools, the county, special districts, and the city in the standard shared proportions.

El Cerrito disputed this determination and litigated it for nearly eight years, ultimately losing when the Court of Appeal affirmed the judgment against the city in March 2021.

“help protect tax increment revenue”
— City staff memorandum, as quoted in the Court of Appeal opinion, El Cerrito Redevelopment Agency Successor Agency v. Bosler, No. C078064

That contemporaneous staff language — describing the purpose of the February 2011 agreement as protecting tax increment revenue — is central to why the courts treated this as exactly the kind of transaction the dissolution law’s asset-transfer rules were designed to catch.

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 6 — Understanding the Two Numbers: $1.98 Million and $1.32 Million
text:
Part 6 — Understanding the Two Numbers: $1.98 Million and $1.32 Million
These two figures are frequently confused, so it is worth explaining the relationship carefully.






TipA Simple Analogy



Imagine the state sends El Cerrito’s Successor Agency a bill for $1.98 million, like a collection notice: “you owe this, full stop.” But the Successor Agency has no independent income of its own — it only receives periodic property-tax distributions tied to already-approved obligations. So the City’s General Fund — the same pot of money that pays for police, parks, and streets — stepped in and fronted cash so the state’s installment payments could be made on schedule, the way a parent might front money for a grown child’s debt with the expectation of eventually being paid back. Each time the General Fund fronted more money, it created and grew an internal IOU: “Successor Agency owes the City’s General Fund.” By 2018, once all the state installments were paid, that internal IOU had grown to $1,321,189. When the 2021 appeal failed and it became clear the Successor Agency would never have independent means to repay it, the City wrote that internal IOU off.


In other words:

$1,981,989 = the total amount owed to the State of California, fully repaid by 2018 using a combination of Successor Agency property-tax distributions, a separate $350,000 loan from the MSC, and proceeds from selling former RDA property.
$1,321,189 = the portion of that repayment effort the City’s General Fund personally fronted, which was never repaid internally and was formally written off as a loss in FY2020-21.

The City’s FY2020-21 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR), Note 16, is explicit that the write-off “has no impact on City cash,” because the cash had already left the General Fund years earlier when it was originally advanced. The write-off was not a second payment to the state — it was a formal accounting acknowledgment that an internal loan would never be collected.
It would therefore be inaccurate to add these two figures together and describe El Cerrito’s loss as $3.3 million. It is more accurate to say: the state recovered $1.98 million total, and of the City resources used to make that happen, $1.32 million came from the General Fund and was never recovered internally.

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 7 — Was This Fair? Two Separate Questions
text:
Part 7 — Was This Fair? Two Separate Questions
“Was this fair to El Cerrito” is really two different questions with two different answers.

Question A: Was the state’s general decision to abolish redevelopment fair to cities?
This is a legitimate, still-debated policy question without a single correct answer.
The case that it was unfair to cities:

Cities had built long-term development programs — for El Cerrito, San Pablo Avenue revitalization — around a financing tool the state then eliminated with about a year’s notice.
El Cerrito’s own budget documents estimate roughly $1 million per year in lost General Fund support for economic development and related City functions in the years immediately following dissolution, reflecting City functions and staff positions the RDA had previously funded.
The state effectively changed the rules after substantial local planning and financial commitments had already been made.

The case that it was justified:

RDAs statewide had grown to capture an increasing, uncapped share of property tax growth, at the direct expense of schools, counties, and other public services.
Because of Proposition 98’s school-funding guarantee, the state itself bore a growing financial burden as a result of RDA tax-increment diversion, making this a genuine state fiscal problem, not merely local politics.
The California Supreme Court upheld the Legislature’s authority to abolish RDAs in California Redevelopment Assn. v. Matosantos (2011), confirming the state acted within its constitutional authority.

This report does not resolve this policy debate — both sides have documented, legitimate arguments, and reasonable people disagree.


Question B: Was El Cerrito unfairly targeted in the specific $1.98 million dispute?
Here, the documented record points more clearly in one direction.
The strongest argument for El Cerrito:

When El Cerrito signed its February 2011 Cooperation Agreement, ABX1 26 had not yet been enacted (it passed in June 2011) — El Cerrito could argue it was using tools that were legally available at the time.
The MSC was not a private developer or anyone’s personal enterprise; the money was intended to remain devoted to public redevelopment purposes.
Some of the dissolution law’s asset-transfer rules were applied to transactions that occurred before the law itself existed — a retroactivity concern that other cities also litigated.

The strongest argument for the State’s position:

The chronology is difficult to characterize as routine business: El Cerrito’s agreement was signed less than a month after Governor Brown’s public proposal to eliminate RDAs, and the asset transfers followed within weeks.
The contemporaneous City staff memorandum explicitly described the purpose as helping to “protect tax increment revenue” — language that undercuts any claim the agreement was unrelated to the dissolution threat.
The recipient of the transferred assets, the MSC, was found by both the State Controller’s Office and the courts to be financially controlled by the City itself, not an independent third party.
The Court of Appeal upheld the state’s treatment of the transaction, and El Cerrito lost at every stage of litigation.
El Cerrito was not singled out: comparable disputes involving Tracy, Brentwood, Big Bear Lake, and San Bernardino (which used a similar nonprofit-transfer structure at a much larger scale) were litigated on similar grounds, with similar outcomes.

Assessment: The evidence does not establish that City officials acted fraudulently or knowingly violated the law in February 2011 — no source reviewed for this page supports that conclusion. A more precise characterization is that El Cerrito aggressively attempted to preserve local redevelopment resources during a rapidly changing legal environment, using a strategy that a number of other California cities also attempted, and that the courts subsequently determined this strategy was not legally effective under the dissolution statute. That is a materially different claim from “the state unfairly targeted El Cerrito,” and the documented record supports the former more than the latter.

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 8 — Statewide Context: El Cerrito Was Not Alone
text:
Part 8 — Statewide Context: El Cerrito Was Not Alone
Court records show El Cerrito’s situation reflected a broader statewide pattern of cities and RDAs attempting to preserve redevelopment resources between January 2011 (when dissolution was proposed) and June 2011 (when it became law).







City
What Happened




Tracy
Entered agreements committing roughly $4.18 million in tax increment and $2.13 million in bond proceeds to the City after Brown’s January 2011 proposal; paid disputed amounts from its General Fund in December 2015 to obtain a Finding of Completion. (City of Tracy v. Cohen, 3 Cal.App.5th 852 (2016))


Brentwood
Entered a series of agreements with its RDA during February–March 2011 while dissolution was being proposed; litigated similar retroactive clawback treatment. (City of Brentwood v. Campbell, 237 Cal.App.4th 488 (2015))


Big Bear Lake
Adopted a cooperation agreement on June 27, 2011 — one day before the dissolution law was signed — later subjected to the same recovery process. (City of Big Bear Lake v. Cohen, No. C076576 (2017))


San Bernardino
Transferred approximately $108.37 million in assets to a City-connected nonprofit (the San Bernardino Economic Development Corporation) on March 17, 2011, for the stated purpose of protecting RDA resources from elimination; the State Controller determined the transfer was unallowable and ordered it reversed. (State Controller, City of San Bernardino Asset Transfer Review, Mar. 6, 2013)



San Bernardino’s case is the closest structural match to El Cerrito’s: a transfer to a City-connected nonprofit, explicitly justified as protecting RDA resources from elimination, that state auditors determined was not legally effective. The pattern across these cases — proposed elimination, a rapid agreement locking in assets, a transfer to a City-related entity, and a subsequent state clawback — shows El Cerrito’s approach was a widely attempted strategy, not an unusual or isolated maneuver.

title: El Cerrito and the Dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies
section: Part 9 — The Ongoing Legacy: A 2016 Loan Still Being Resolved in 2024
text:
Part 9 — The Ongoing Legacy: A 2016 Loan Still Being Resolved in 2024
One concrete, continuing financial consequence of this dispute persisted more than a decade after the original transaction. To help make the DOF installment payments, the City borrowed $350,000 from the MSC at 0% interest in 2016, originally expecting repayment by around FY2020. As of a City March 5, 2024 Mid-Year Budget Update (Agenda Item 9.B), the City proposed resolving that obligation by appropriating $350,000 of unassigned General Fund balance toward the Del Norte Complete Streets Project, following a November 2023 MSC-accepted proposal to satisfy the loan this way.
This shows the financial consequences of the 2011 transaction and its unwinding reached well beyond the formal 2021 court decision and 2020-21 write-off, continuing to affect General Fund allocation decisions as recently as 2024.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text: A “going concern” opinion is an auditor’s formal statement of substantial doubt about a government’s ability to meet its financial obligations. El Cerrito’s CAFRs/ACFRs contain this language across a specific multi-year period, documented year by year below.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2013 and FY2014

title: California State Auditor Findings
text:
In March 2021, the California State Auditor designated El Cerrito a “high risk” local government in Report 2020-803, titled “Excessive Spending and Insufficient Efforts to Address Its Perilous Financial Condition Jeopardize the City’s Ongoing Fiscal Viability.”
The audit found that El Cerrito spent more than it received in general fund revenue in eight of the eleven fiscal years from 2009–10 through 2019–20, and that its general fund reserves — built up to a peak of $2.6 million in FY2011–12 — were fully depleted by FY2016–17 and remained negative through FY2019–20. The city’s own reserve policy requires a minimum of 10% of expenditures; it did not meet that threshold in any of the eleven years reviewed.

Source: Report 2020-803, Table 1, based on the City’s audited comprehensive annual financial reports, FY2009–10 through FY2019–20. GFOA’s recommended minimum is 17% (two months of expenditures); El Cerrito’s own policy sets a 10% minimum.

The report also found the city relied on short-term loans (TRANs) every year since FY2012–13 to cover operating costs, with the loan amount growing from $5 million in FY2015–16 to a peak of $9 million in FY2019–20. The associated interest rate roughly doubled over that span, and annual interest costs more than tripled. The auditor’s own comparison noted that El Cerrito’s credit rating deteriorated from an AA− rating in 2016 to a BBB− rating in 2020, tracking the decline in reserves.
Other findings included a net pension liability of $65.8 million as of June 2020 (a 67% increase from FY2014–15), and a capital/maintenance backlog of $245.4 million identified in the FY2020–21 budget, of which only $21.4 million was funded through FY2024–25 — a rate the auditor noted would take more than 50 years to address at that pace. The audit also identified budget-monitoring weaknesses, including a finding that finance department staff routinely overrode internal spending-limit alerts without director-level review.

Source: California State Auditor, Report 2020-803, “City of El Cerrito: Excessive Spending and Insufficient Efforts to Address Its Perilous Financial Condition Jeopardize the City’s Ongoing Fiscal Viability,” issued March 16, 2021. Full report | City’s posted response page

title: Measure C
text:
Citizen-initiated ordinance adding Chapter 4.58 to the El Cerrito Municipal Code, authorizing an annual special parcel tax. (Impact Report, p.6)

Maximum initial rate: $0.17 per square foot of improvements; $100 per vacant parcel. (Impact Report, p.6; §4.58.040(A))
Annual escalator: up to the greater of Bay Area CPI or CA per-capita personal income growth, at Council’s discretion (not automatic). (Impact Report, p.6; §4.58.040(B))
Secondary statutory cap: total annual levy may not exceed 115% of revenue needed for (1) construction-debt service and (2) library operating costs for the first 10 years post-construction. (Impact Report, p.6–7; §4.58.040(C))
Use of funds: planning, permitting, environmental review, construction, and furnishing of a new library, plus up to 10 years of City library operating costs. (Impact Report, p.6–7; §4.58.060(A))
Duration: 30 years from the initial issuance of bonds for the library. (Impact Report, p.11; §4.58.110)
Projected gross annual revenue at maximum rates: $3,156,019 (rounded publicly to “~$3.1M”), based on 18,458,937 taxable building sq ft + 180 vacant parcels, FY2025-26 property profile. (Impact Report, p.18)
Average residential parcel: 1,946 sq ft → ~$331 projected initial annual tax. (Impact Report, p.18)
Exemptions: owners qualifying for the state’s Gonzalez-Deukmejian-Petris Senior Citizen Property Tax Assistance Law or the Senior Citizen Property Tax Postponement Law. (Impact Report, p.9–10; §4.58.030(C)(3))
Oversight: annual independent-audit review referred to a citizen oversight board (existing or new), designated by Council. (Impact Report, p.10; §4.58.080)
Vote threshold: simple majority (citizen-initiative case law), not two-thirds. (Impact Report, p.2)
